chapters.title: Orientation, Training Expectations and Careers
prompts: Describe how online theory, workbook responses, observed practical skills, and the external EPA exam provide different evidence. Build your personal completion checklist.
Draw your learning sequence and mark which activities require an instructor. Explain why course completion is not EPA certification.
Write three questions for your instructor about equipment access, the exam version, and your hands-on schedule.
chapters.heading: Build an evidence-based learning plan
chapters.text: Organize a training binder into four parts: theory, workbook, assessed practice, and supervised performance. For theory, retain the lesson title and questions you can explain without looking. In the workbook, show your reasoning and units; a correct number without an explanation is incomplete learning evidence. In practice assessments, use incorrect answers to identify a topic to revisit. For supervised performance, record the actual task, equipment, date, and authorized assessor. These records answer different questions. A quiz demonstrates knowledge under its assessment conditions. A practical observation demonstrates what someone actually saw you do. Neither automatically establishes an external credential. Plan a short study session around one objective: read, describe the diagram aloud, work an example, complete a different example independently, and review the difference. Stop studying a paragraph passively if you cannot explain the concept in your own words.
chapters.example: A student watches the electrical lesson and writes that current equals voltage divided by resistance. The student then calculates 24 V / 12 ohms = 2 A and explains that this describes an idealized resistive load. That is stronger evidence than copying the formula, but it is still not permission to test energized equipment.
chapters.review: Check that your plan includes time for corrections, instructor questions, and the separate practical appointment.

lessons.heading: Understand the purpose and limits of this course
lessons.text: This course connects heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigerant-handling concepts with supervised occupational practice. The online lessons explain decisions and prepare you to recognize components, interpret information and identify safe next steps. Practical competence requires the actual observed tasks and check-offs specified by the program. Passing an online quiz or watching a photograph-based film does not show that you can safely service equipment. Review the course sequence, the instructions for each assessment and the practical evidence required before you begin work on a live system.

lessons.heading: Connect the main HVAC functions and career roles
lessons.text: Heating adds heat to a space; cooling removes heat from it. Ventilation brings or exchanges air according to the building's design, while distribution moves conditioned air or another heat-transfer medium to where it is needed. Refrigeration uses a working fluid and equipment to move heat between locations. Residential work commonly involves homes, while commercial and industrial work can involve larger or specialized systems. Installation, maintenance and service roles share a need for accurate documentation, communication and problem solving, but the equipment and qualifications vary. A job title does not itself establish authority to perform every task.

lessons.heading: Follow the lesson sequence and maintain evidence
lessons.text: Begin with system operation and safety, then study electrical fundamentals, heating and the refrigeration cycle. The refrigerant lessons distinguish environmental requirements, recovery decisions and the equipment categories used in Section 608 certification. Later lessons connect measurements, installation, troubleshooting and customer communication. For each lesson, retain your worked examples, assessment results, corrections and required practical records. Use the program's actual attendance, pacing and submission rules. If a schedule, access problem or support need affects participation, contact the designated program staff early. Do not invent attendance, backdate practice or record an unobserved skill as completed.

lessons.heading: Worked example: separate learning from a credential
lessons.text: An enrolled learner completes the online refrigerant lessons and passes the internal practice assessment. The learner can accurately report completion of those course activities, but cannot describe that result as an EPA credential unless the separate approved examination has been passed and the credential is documented. Section 608 certification is earned through an EPA-approved testing organization for the relevant equipment category. EPA also describes an apprentice exemption tied to close and continual supervision by a certified technician. That exception is not general permission for an unqualified learner to work alone or perform unrelated electrical, combustion or other hazardous tasks.

lessons.heading: Build your training readiness plan
lessons.text: Create a checklist showing the lesson order, assessment instructions, required practical observations, external examinations and the staff member responsible for each question. Record credentials as verified, pending or not yet attempted. Review your access to the approved learning platform, safe training equipment and qualified supervision. If seeking financial assistance or support services, ask the responsible provider for its actual eligibility and approval process; enrollment does not guarantee funding or employment. Submit a short explanation of one HVAC career role, one task requiring further qualification and one action you will take when a safety instruction or program requirement is unclear.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: System Operation, Tools, Components and Shop Safety
prompts: Draw a cooling system and label compressor, condenser, metering device, and evaporator. Add arrows showing refrigerant flow.
Create a tool-identification table: multimeter, thermometer, scale, vacuum gauge, recovery machine. Describe the measurement or task each supports.
For a damaged lead, unknown refrigerant, and missing eye protection, explain why you stop and whom you contact before supervised work.
chapters.heading: Read a system as connected functions
chapters.text: A component name is useful only when you can explain its job and connections. In the cooling model, electrical power operates the compressor and fans, refrigerant moves heat between coils, and air carries heat between a coil and the space. A malfunction in any one path can change the observations in another. Reduced airflow can change coil temperature and refrigerant readings; this does not prove a refrigerant shortage. Map the three paths separately before joining them. Identify where energy enters and leaves, which measurements could test a proposed explanation, and which safety controls are needed before measurement. A multimeter measures electrical quantities within its selected function and rating. A temperature probe measures temperature at a specific location. A refrigerant scale measures mass. A vacuum gauge assesses pressure in an appropriate range. None of these instruments substitutes for the others. Record the instrument, range, units, connection location, and manufacturer procedure for the assigned task.
chapters.example: A room is warm, the blower is running, and a filter is visibly obstructed. The supported observation is an airflow restriction that requires investigation. The unsupported conclusion is that the system needs refrigerant. Write the airflow observation first and identify the next authorized inspection.
chapters.review: Explain which tool provides each measurement and one limitation of its result.

lessons.heading: Trace the system's function before choosing a tool
lessons.text: An HVAC system combines equipment, controls and distribution to serve a building's heating, cooling and ventilation needs. Identify the actual equipment and operating mode before interpreting what a component should do. A thermostat or controller requests operation; it does not replace the equipment's protective controls. Fans or blowers move air, heat exchangers transfer heat, and ducts or piping distribute the useful result. In a vapor-compression cooling circuit, the compressor, condenser, metering device and evaporator perform different functions. Airflow problems, control faults and refrigerant-side problems can produce similar comfort complaints, so a symptom alone is not a diagnosis.

lessons.heading: Recognize the main refrigeration components
lessons.text: The compressor receives refrigerant vapor and raises its pressure while circulating it through the circuit. In the condenser, refrigerant rejects heat and can change from vapor toward liquid as it passes through the heat exchanger. The metering device controls refrigerant flow into the lower-pressure side. In the evaporator, refrigerant absorbs heat as it evaporates. A heat pump can change which coil supplies heating or cooling to the occupied space. Use the actual diagram and operating mode to label a coil's role; do not assume an indoor coil is always an evaporator under every condition.

lessons.heading: Match the instrument to the question and hazard
lessons.text: A temperature instrument measures temperature, a pressure instrument measures pressure, and a multimeter can measure the electrical quantities supported by its design and selected function. A clamp instrument measures current in the manner specified by its manufacturer. Recovery equipment removes refrigerant to an appropriate external container; it is not automatically a complete recycling or reclamation system. Select compatible tools with the required ratings and inspect them before use. Read the appliance nameplate, tool instructions and relevant safety data. A brand name is not an adequate refrigerant identification, and the appearance of a connection does not prove compatibility.

lessons.heading: Worked example: inspect a training system safely
lessons.text: A training air conditioner has weak airflow and poor cooling. Before proposing refrigerant charging, review the operating conditions, service information and safe inspection plan with the instructor. On a deenergized training display, identify the blower, filter location, coils, compressor and metering device. Explain how an airflow restriction could affect performance and why the complaint alone does not establish a low charge. Electrical isolation must follow the employer's applicable procedure, with the required verification by a qualified person. A thermostat in the off position is not proof that hazardous energy has been isolated.

lessons.heading: Complete a supervised component and safety map
lessons.text: Create a labeled system map showing the purpose of each major component, the operating mode and the instrument that could answer one defined diagnostic question. Identify electrical energy, pressure, sharp metal, rotating parts, hot surfaces and any refrigerant-specific ignition or exposure hazard before practice. State the required isolation, protective equipment and stop conditions from the actual instructions and task assessment. Do not open a circuit, connect gauges, bypass a safety or perform an energized test merely to complete this worksheet. Have the instructor observe component identification and verify that your proposed next step fits your qualification and the training conditions.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: Electrical Fundamentals, Wiring and Diagnostic Instruments
prompts: Sketch a simple 24-volt source, switch, and load circuit. Predict current flow when the switch is open and closed.
Calculate current for a hypothetical 24 V circuit with 12 ohms of resistance. Show I = V/R and explain why this is an idealized exercise.
Compare measuring voltage in parallel with measuring resistance on isolated equipment. Describe the instructor-approved safe setup; do not work on live equipment for this exercise.
chapters.heading: Connect circuit behavior to a measurement plan
chapters.text: Voltage is electrical potential difference, current is charge flow, and resistance opposes that flow. A complete circuit needs a source, conductors, a load, and a return path. An open switch interrupts its series path; a closed switch permits a complete path when the rest of the circuit is intact. In an ideal resistive example, Ohm's law is V = I times R. Rearrange before inserting numbers: I = V/R and R = V/I. Power for the same ideal model is P = V times I. Do not apply a simple resistance model blindly to motor starting or other alternating-current behavior. A control circuit and a line-voltage power circuit can interact while operating at different voltages. Trace the schematic rather than guessing from wire color. Voltage measurements compare two points; resistance tests need the approved isolated, de-energized setup. Work only on the instructor's safe training rig under its procedure. A model in this workbook never authorizes opening an energized panel.
chapters.example: For a hypothetical 24 V source and 12-ohm resistor, I = 24/12 = 2 A and P = 24 times 2 = 48 W. If resistance becomes 24 ohms while voltage stays 24 V, current becomes 1 A. If the switch opens, the series-path current is zero in this ideal model.
chapters.review: Show the rearranged formula, substitution, result, and units. Compare an open path with a higher-resistance complete path.

lessons.heading: Use voltage, current and resistance precisely
lessons.text: Voltage is an electrical potential difference measured in volts. Current is the rate of electric charge flow, measured in amperes. Resistance is opposition to current in the resistive model, measured in ohms. For a basic resistive circuit, Ohm's law relates these quantities as voltage equals current multiplied by resistance. Rearranging gives current equals voltage divided by resistance, and resistance equals voltage divided by current. Keep the units and assumptions visible. Real alternating-current motor circuits can involve reactance and other behavior, so a simplified resistor exercise is not a complete diagnostic model for every HVAC load.

lessons.heading: Worked example: calculate before interpreting
lessons.text: For an ideal ten-ohm resistor connected to a 120-volt source in a hypothetical calculation, current is 120 divided by ten, or twelve amperes. An answer of five amperes does not follow those stated values. For a second ideal resistor of twelve ohms at 24 volts, current is two amperes. In that simple resistive example, electrical power is voltage multiplied by current, or 48 watts. These are paper calculations, not directions to assemble or energize a circuit. A correct calculation still requires a suitable model, verified inputs and an explanation of what the result means.

lessons.heading: Read diagrams and identify the actual instrument function
lessons.text: A schematic emphasizes how the circuit functions; a wiring or connection diagram helps identify how actual components are connected. Read the legend, device labels, terminal markings and model-specific documentation rather than assuming every manufacturer uses the same symbol or wire color. Trace the supply, protective devices, switching elements and load on a deenergized training diagram. A contactor switches a power circuit under its designed control, while a relay performs its specified switching role. A capacitor stores electrical energy and must be treated according to the actual equipment instructions, including the hazard from stored energy after a supply is disconnected.

lessons.heading: Choose the test from a safe, qualified plan
lessons.text: A multimeter must have the appropriate rating, leads, connection method and selected function for the measurement. Voltage may be alternating or direct, so DC voltage is not the correct universal setting for every voltage test. Resistance measurements require the appropriate deenergized conditions and procedure; do not apply an ohmmeter indiscriminately to an energized circuit. A clamp meter also has model-specific limits and instructions. Only qualified people may perform energized work under the applicable requirements. Learners should begin with paper diagrams and instructor-approved deenergized trainers, with isolation and absence-of-voltage verification handled through the required qualified procedure.

lessons.heading: Practice, stop conditions and recap
lessons.text: Complete both resistor calculations, label a basic schematic and explain the selected meter function for a hypothetical AC voltage question and a hypothetical resistance question. Identify damaged leads, an unknown rating, uncertain isolation, exposed energized parts and stored energy as reasons to pause and obtain qualified guidance. Do not remove another person's lock, defeat an interlock or improvise a capacitor discharge method. Have the instructor verify your reasoning and observe any permitted practical task under the actual training plan. Record measured values only when a real authorized measurement occurred, and separate them from calculated or assumed values in your notes.

chapters.imageAlt: Technician Testing Industrial Air Conditioning with Multimeter

chapters.title: Furnaces, Electric Heat, Heat Pumps and Combustion
prompts: Compare electric resistance heating, a gas furnace, and a heat pump: energy input, heat source, and major components.
Draw a heat-pump heating-mode diagram. Explain how indoor and outdoor coil roles differ from cooling mode.
List combustion, electrical, and refrigerant hazards that require qualified supervision. Draft a stop-work response to a suspected carbon-monoxide hazard.
chapters.heading: Compare heating mechanisms and heat-pump modes
chapters.text: Electric resistance heat converts electrical energy to heat at an element. A combustion furnace transfers heat from controlled combustion through a heat exchanger while combustion products follow their designed venting path. A heat pump transfers heat between locations using the refrigerant cycle; it does not produce all of its delivered heat by resistance alone. In a reversible heat pump, coil roles change with operating mode. In heating mode, the indoor coil normally rejects heat to indoor air and the outdoor coil absorbs heat from outdoors. The compressor still receives the appropriate vapor condition and discharges high-pressure vapor. Controls, defrost operation, auxiliary heat, airflow, and environmental conditions affect system behavior. A cold outdoor coil alone does not establish a fault. For any heating investigation, identify the equipment, operating mode, control call, measured conditions, and manufacturer sequence before interpreting symptoms. Combustion, electrical, rotating equipment, and refrigerant hazards demand qualified procedures.
chapters.example: A learner labels the indoor coil 'evaporator' in every operating mode. Correct the diagram by function: the indoor coil is the condenser during the illustrated heating mode. Explain that the reversing valve changes routing, while component function must be read from the current mode.
chapters.review: Compare where heat originates in a furnace, a resistance heater, and a heat pump.

lessons.heading: Identify the source of heat
lessons.text: A heating call does not tell you how an appliance produces heat. Read the nameplate and manufacturer service information before forming a diagnosis. A gas furnace releases heat through controlled combustion and transfers that heat through a heat exchanger to the circulating air. Electric resistance heat converts electrical energy into heat in resistance elements. A heat pump moves heat using a refrigerant circuit; auxiliary resistance heat may supplement its output. Record the equipment model, fuel or electrical supply, controls and any auxiliary heating equipment. Distinguishing these systems helps you choose relevant observations instead of applying a furnace troubleshooting sequence to every heating complaint.

lessons.heading: Trace the intended sequence
lessons.text: Compare the observed operating sequence with the exact equipment instructions. A furnace may require an inducer, pressure proving, ignition and flame proving before sustained heating and blower operation; the timing and components vary. Resistance heating involves controls, protective devices and potentially multiple heating stages. A heat pump uses refrigerant flow to deliver heat indoors and may change operation during defrost. Thermostat settings, airflow and outdoor conditions affect the complaint. A normal defrost event should not automatically be called a compressor failure. Describe what was observed, when it occurred and which expected step failed, rather than guessing a failed component from one sound.

lessons.heading: Recognize conditions that require stopping
lessons.text: Combustion equipment can create carbon-monoxide and fire hazards. Electrical circuits, capacitors, moving blowers and hot surfaces create additional hazards across heating technologies. An alarm, suspected gas leak, damaged wiring, abnormal combustion evidence or unsafe access calls for the applicable emergency or site procedure and qualified help. Do not bypass an interlock, defeat a limit switch or repeatedly reset a tripping protective device to keep heat running. Electrical work requires the applicable deenergization and lockout procedures and verification by a qualified person. An introductory course does not qualify a learner to conduct energized testing, adjust combustion or declare an occupied building safe.

lessons.heading: Work through a heating complaint
lessons.text: A customer reports that a heat pump blows cooler-feeling air than a previous gas furnace. Begin by recording room temperature, thermostat demand, equipment identification, outdoor conditions and the customer's description. Cooler-feeling supply air alone does not prove that the heat pump is failing: the technologies can deliver different supply-air temperatures. Compare measured performance with the manufacturer procedure, airflow requirements and operating conditions. If auxiliary heat is installed, verify its commanded stages and documented sequence through authorized testing. Explain that a diagnosis requires evidence. Do not promise that adding refrigerant will fix the complaint or recommend replacing the system before checking the relevant operating data.

lessons.heading: Practice the comparison and document limits
lessons.text: Prepare a three-column comparison for gas combustion, resistance heat and heat-pump heating. For each, name the heat source, one normal operating observation, two hazards and the document that controls service checks. Then write a service note for the customer scenario: reported concern, facts collected, additional authorized checks needed and a clear next step. Keep suspected causes separate from confirmed findings. Ask your instructor to review the sequence and the points at which the work must stop. Completing this written exercise records your reasoning; it does not substitute for supervised practical assessment, an electrical qualification, a combustion analysis or an external safety credential.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: Refrigeration Cycle, Pressure, Superheat and Subcooling
prompts: Use the animated cycle. Record refrigerant state, relative pressure, and heat direction at all four components. Explain why compressor discharge is vapor.

At the virtual bench, calculate superheat from 50°F suction-line temperature and 40°F evaporating saturation temperature, and subcooling from 105°F condensing saturation and 95°F liquid-line temperature.
Change one virtual reading at a time. Explain the result, the assumed phase, and why readings alone do not justify adding refrigerant.
chapters.heading: Interpret superheat, subcooling, and blend references
chapters.text: At a specified pressure, saturation is the temperature associated with a phase change for the identified refrigerant. Superheat compares vapor-line temperature with the appropriate saturation temperature at the same relevant pressure location. Subcooling compares the appropriate liquid-side saturation temperature with the measured liquid temperature. Pressure loss between measurement points can invalidate an otherwise correct calculation. For a zeotropic blend with temperature glide, vapor-side superheat normally uses dew-point data and liquid-side subcooling uses bubble-point data. Confirm the refrigerant and chart convention. A numerical difference is not a charging recommendation. Metering device type, load, airflow, measurement accuracy, and the manufacturer's target method affect interpretation. Use the virtual bench to change one variable while holding the others fixed; this isolates the arithmetic relationship without pretending a real system has no interacting effects. A negative calculated value challenges the assumed outlet phase or measurement reference and needs investigation.
chapters.example: With an appropriate dew saturation temperature of 42 F and vapor-line temperature of 56 F, superheat is 14 F. With bubble saturation at 108 F and liquid at 99 F, subcooling is 9 F. If the two temperatures came from incompatible locations or a different refrigerant chart, the numerical answers would not establish a valid system interpretation.
chapters.review: State why a calculation can be mathematically correct but diagnostically unsupported.

lessons.heading: Follow the four principal components
lessons.text: In a basic vapor-compression cooling cycle, the compressor takes in low-pressure refrigerant vapor and raises its pressure and temperature. The condenser rejects heat and condenses refrigerant toward a high-pressure liquid condition. The metering device restricts flow and reduces pressure. The evaporator absorbs heat as refrigerant boils at the lower pressure. Follow the tubing and heat flow rather than memorizing component names in isolation. Indoor cooling means heat is being removed from the conditioned space and rejected elsewhere. A heat pump can reverse which coil serves as the evaporator and condenser; the compressor still requires the correct inlet vapor condition.

lessons.heading: Use the correct pressure-temperature relationship
lessons.text: Pressure alone is not a universal temperature or a complete diagnosis. Identify the refrigerant from reliable equipment information and select the appropriate pressure-temperature data. At saturation, pressure and temperature are related for that refrigerant. Some blends require different dew-point and bubble-point values when calculating superheat and subcooling. Gauge pressure and absolute pressure are different quantities, so verify the chart and instrument conventions. Record the refrigerant, measurement location, operating mode and units. Never substitute another refrigerant's chart because the pressures look familiar, and never treat a single generic pressure target as correct for every system or outdoor condition.

lessons.heading: Calculate superheat from paired measurements
lessons.text: Superheat is the measured vapor temperature minus the saturation temperature corresponding to the pressure at the relevant location. For a hypothetical example, assume verified refrigerant data gives a saturation temperature of 40 degrees Fahrenheit and the properly measured vapor-line temperature at the corresponding point is 52 degrees Fahrenheit. The calculated superheat is 12 Fahrenheit degrees. This arithmetic does not establish that 12 degrees is the correct target for the appliance. Target methods depend on the metering device, operating conditions and manufacturer instructions. Pressure and temperature measurements from different locations can mislead because pressure changes along a system.

lessons.heading: Calculate subcooling and interpret cautiously
lessons.text: Subcooling is the saturation temperature for the relevant liquid-side pressure minus the measured liquid temperature at the corresponding location. If the appropriate saturation value is 110 degrees Fahrenheit and the liquid measures 100 degrees Fahrenheit, the calculated subcooling is 10 Fahrenheit degrees. Again, this is an arithmetic example, not a universal charging target. Interpret both measurements with airflow, load, operating mode and equipment specifications. Poor airflow, instrument error and operating conditions can affect readings. Do not add or remove refrigerant merely because one reading differs from an example in a lesson. Refrigerant handling requires the applicable qualification and compatible equipment.

lessons.heading: Practice a complete measurement record
lessons.text: Draw the four-component cycle and label the direction of heat transfer at each coil in cooling mode. Beside it, work two calculation problems: vapor at 58 degrees with a corresponding saturation value of 43 gives 15 degrees of superheat; a liquid-side saturation value of 105 with measured liquid at 97 gives 8 degrees of subcooling. State what information is still needed before judging either result acceptable. Include refrigerant identity, chart convention, paired measurement locations, operating conditions and the manufacturer's target method. Review the calculations with an instructor. This paper exercise develops interpretation skills and does not authorize opening a live refrigerant circuit or conducting unsupervised service.

chapters.imageAlt: Technician Testing Industrial Air Conditioning with Multimeter

chapters.title: Environmental Protection, Section 608 and Refrigerant Safety
prompts: Build a Core vocabulary sheet distinguishing CFC, HCFC, HFC, ozone-depletion potential, and global-warming potential. Use official EPA references and identify one example refrigerant in each family.
Explain the Montreal Protocol and Clean Air Act in your own words. Distinguish production phaseout from a blanket ban on servicing existing equipment.
Classify a factory-manufactured, charged, hermetically sealed four-pound appliance and a field-assembled four-pound system. Explain why charge weight alone is insufficient.
chapters.heading: Core reference: environment, refrigerant families, and oils
chapters.text: Chlorine released from certain refrigerants in the stratosphere contributes to ozone depletion. CFCs and HCFCs contain chlorine; HFCs do not. R-12 is a CFC, R-22 an HCFC, and R-134a an HFC. Zero ozone-depletion potential does not imply zero global-warming impact or zero safety hazard. The Montreal Protocol is an international agreement addressing ozone-depleting substances; the Clean Air Act provides the United States legal framework for requirements including refrigerant management. United States production and import of most CFCs ended in 1996, and production and import of new R-22 for servicing ended in 2020; these dates are not a blanket order to discard every existing system. Refrigerant replacement requires applicable approval and equipment compatibility. Oil choice also matters: mineral, alkylbenzene, and polyolester oils are not interchangeable simply because all lubricate. POE oils readily absorb moisture, so storage and handling controls matter. Use the compressor and refrigerant manufacturers' requirements. Blend components can behave differently during leaks and phase change, producing fractionation. Identify blend composition and appropriate charging instructions rather than assuming a mixture behaves like a pure refrigerant.
chapters.example: A label identifies R-134a. The learner correctly identifies it as an HFC, then incorrectly concludes that deliberate release is allowed because it contains no chlorine. Correct the reasoning: ozone chemistry, climate effect, and the applicable venting prohibition are separate questions.
chapters.review: Distinguish refrigerant family, safety classification, environmental effect, and appliance certification category.

lessons.heading: Separate ozone impact from climate impact
lessons.text: Ozone depletion and climate warming describe different environmental effects. A refrigerant can have no ozone-depletion potential and still contribute to climate warming when released. An environmental label does not make a refrigerant harmless, establish appliance compatibility or permit deliberate release. Identify the actual refrigerant and the regulations relevant to the service activity. Connect environmental responsibility to concrete work habits: keep refrigerant contained, maintain identification, use appropriate recovery equipment and document the required information. Avoid selecting a replacement only because its environmental rating sounds better. Its permitted use and compatibility with the equipment must also be established.

lessons.heading: Match certification scope to the appliance
lessons.text: Type I covers small appliances. The complete definition requires factory manufacture, factory charging and hermetic sealing with five pounds or less of refrigerant. Type II covers high- and very-high-pressure appliances except small appliances and motor vehicle air conditioners. Type III covers low-pressure appliances. Universal covers all three categories. Neither a five-pound minimum nor a fifty-pound minimum defines the Type II or Type III certification category. Section 609 addresses motor vehicle air conditioning and has a separate scope. Completing this course does not itself issue an EPA credential; the approved examination and its applicable certification requirements remain separate.

lessons.heading: Identify hazards from actual documents
lessons.text: Before a refrigerant task, obtain the nameplate information, equipment instructions and applicable safety data sheet. Refrigerants can involve pressure, cold-liquid injury, oxygen displacement and, for some substances, ignition hazards. Select controls, compatible equipment and personal protection for the actual substance and task. A generic face covering does not protect against oxygen deficiency, and a fitting connection does not establish chemical or pressure compatibility. Stop if the refrigerant cannot be reliably identified or if the required equipment, ventilation, safe work area or qualification is missing. Do not resolve uncertainty by mixing refrigerants, improvising a container or using an undocumented service procedure.

lessons.heading: Work through the small-charge classification example
lessons.text: An instructor supplies information for two stationary systems, each with a four-pound charge. One is fully manufactured, charged and hermetically sealed in a factory; the other is field assembled. The first may meet the small-appliance definition when all the supplied facts are verified. The second cannot be placed in that category from charge weight alone. Explain which additional classification information is needed for the field-assembled equipment. Then consider a low-pressure chiller: identify the Type III scope without inventing a charge minimum. This exercise tests the category definition, not the learner's ability to open or operate the equipment.

lessons.heading: Practice a defensible pre-service decision
lessons.text: Prepare an identification sheet for a supplied appliance example. Record its model, refrigerant, charge information, construction and category evidence, required technician scope and the documents that govern equipment selection and hazards. Identify the recovery and container information you would need before supervised service. Where evidence is absent, write a clear stop condition and the information needed to continue. Review the sheet with the instructor and correct any assumption that comes from cabinet size, price or environmental branding alone. Keep the reasoning exercise, observed practical check-offs and external examination results as separate records of what has actually been learned or verified.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: Recovery Principles, Sales Rules and Core Practice
prompts: Draw three labeled boxes for recover, recycle, and reclaim. Explain what each establishes and what it does not establish.

Prepare a cylinder-safety and transport research checklist covering identification, approved reusable containers, fill limits, and shipping labels. Cite the current source used; do not improvise a fill procedure.
Compare system-dependent and self-contained recovery. Identify which appliance and recovery-equipment facts must be known before selecting a method.
chapters.heading: Core reference: recovery containers, processing, and transport
chapters.text: Recovery captures refrigerant into an external container. Recycling removes some contaminants through processes such as oil separation and filtration. Reclamation processes refrigerant to the required purity specification and includes verification; a recovery machine alone does not establish that purity. An EPA-certified reclaimer is required when applicable recovered refrigerant changes ownership. A self-contained recovery machine supplies its own means of removing refrigerant; system-dependent recovery relies on appliance components or pressure. Recovery equipment must be compatible and appropriately certified. Use approved refillable recovery cylinders, maintain identification, and never refill a disposable cylinder. Yellow-and-gray recovery-cylinder identification does not by itself prove the cylinder is suitable or within its inspection requirements. The familiar 80-percent liquid-volume rule leaves expansion space; it is not permission to fill every cylinder to 80 percent of an arbitrary scale number. Use the cylinder markings, water capacity, tare weight, refrigerant properties, approved fill calculation, and equipment procedure. Shipping requires the correct refrigerant identification, hazard classification, labels, and transport compliance. Never mix refrigerants to save container space.
chapters.example: Two cylinders have equal outside dimensions but different markings and contents. A learner proposes the same gross fill weight for both. Explain why external size is insufficient and identify the container and refrigerant data needed before an authorized person determines the permitted fill.
chapters.review: Explain why cylinder appearance, fitting compatibility, and a successful recovery do not establish safe reuse or shipping compliance.

lessons.heading: Distinguish recovery from cleaning and reclamation
lessons.text: Recovery removes refrigerant from an appliance and stores it in an external container. It does not by itself prove that the contents meet every requirement for reuse. Recycling and reclamation describe different processing and purity frameworks; use the applicable definitions when deciding what recovered refrigerant may be used for. Keep the refrigerant identity and ownership information available rather than treating every recovered cylinder as interchangeable stock. Do not assume an unknown mixture is acceptable because pressure appears normal. The service decision needs reliable identification, compatible equipment and the requirements for the intended use, not merely evidence that refrigerant was captured.

lessons.heading: Plan containment before opening the circuit
lessons.text: Identify the appliance, refrigerant, charge and applicable recovery requirement before choosing a procedure. Confirm the recovery equipment's required certification and compatibility and inspect the container's identification, condition and permitted use. Follow the actual manufacturer instructions and the applicable service rules. Deliberately venting regulated refrigerant for easier disassembly is not an acceptable shortcut. A small incidental release associated with a good-faith service connection does not authorize discharging the rest of the system into the air. Plan how recovered contents will remain identified and separated. Stop when essential identification, safe equipment or a suitable container is missing.

lessons.heading: Apply sales rules to the actual transaction
lessons.text: Refrigerant purchase restrictions depend on the applicable rules, refrigerant and purchaser's documented status, including specified exceptions. Appropriately certified technicians and qualifying employers or authorized representatives must follow the relevant purchasing requirements. Do not invent an exemption from the size of an arbitrary cylinder. Motor vehicle air-conditioning certification under Section 609 is not a blanket authorization for stationary-equipment refrigerant purchases. Consult EPA's current sales guidance for the actual transaction and retain the documentation it requires. A supplier's willingness to make a sale does not establish that the planned equipment use or service task is compatible, permitted or within the technician's qualification.

lessons.heading: Evaluate a replacement request using evidence
lessons.text: A customer asks for an unknown refrigerant to be replaced with whichever product is cheapest. Explain why price is insufficient to choose the action. Identify the appliance and its documented refrigerant, determine the permitted service or conversion options, verify qualification and select compatible equipment before planning the work. A lower global-warming potential alone does not make a substitute an automatic drop-in replacement. If a leak is suspected, adding refrigerant is not a diagnosis and does not locate the fault. Give the customer a clear next step that separates identification and investigation from an unverified promise of a simple replacement.

lessons.heading: Practice the recovery and purchase decision record
lessons.text: For a classroom scenario, list the records needed to support three decisions: the recovery requirement, the permitted handling of the recovered contents and the purchaser's authorization. Include equipment identification, refrigerant identity, recovery machine and container information, applicable instructions and the relevant official sales source. Describe what you would do if a label is missing or a proposed container's suitability cannot be verified. Identify at least one prohibited shortcut and explain the correct reasoning. Review your record with the instructor and retain the corrected version. The exercise is evidence of knowledge; live recovery and external certification need their own verified practical and examination records.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: Small Appliances: Recovery Equipment, Procedures and Practice
prompts: Draw the Type I decision tree using recovery-equipment date and appliance-compressor condition. Include the applicable percentage and vacuum alternatives from EPA guidance.
For a ten-ounce example charge, calculate ninety percent and eighty percent. Explain why arithmetic alone does not verify the required recovery procedure.

Sketch high-side and low-side access points on a hypothetical small appliance. Ask your trainer to demonstrate the actual approved recovery setup and record questions; do not perform unsupervised service.
chapters.heading: Type I: choose a recovery target and interpret the setup
chapters.text: Small-appliance classification requires all the factory conditions and no more than five pounds of charge. Select the recovery requirement using the recovery equipment's manufacture date and the appliance compressor's condition. For equipment manufactured before November 15, 1993, the percentage requirement is 80 percent. For later equipment, it is 90 percent when the appliance compressor functions and 80 percent when it does not. Four inches Hg vacuum is an alternative described in EPA guidance. Percentage of charge and pressure are different measurement concepts. A system-dependent setup uses the appliance or its internal pressure to support recovery; a self-contained machine has its own recovery mechanism. An inoperative compressor can trap refrigerant in different parts of a system, so the approved procedure may require access to both sides. Do not improvise heating, access fittings, or connections from an illustration. A pressure-temperature comparison can help identify noncondensables when refrigerant identity and equilibrium conditions are established; pressure alone cannot reliably identify an unknown mixture. Remove temporary access arrangements as required by the actual equipment procedure.
chapters.example: The instructor supplies a factory-sealed appliance with ten ounces of refrigerant and post-1993 recovery equipment. With a working compressor, 90 percent corresponds to nine ounces. With a nonworking compressor, 80 percent corresponds to eight ounces. Explain both the decision branch and the limits of using a mass arithmetic example as practical evidence.
chapters.review: Identify which date belongs to recovery equipment and why a small field-assembled charge is not automatically Type I.

lessons.heading: Guided instruction
lessons.text: Type I preparation focuses on identifying small appliances and applying the correct recovery decision. A small appliance is fully manufactured, charged, and hermetically sealed in a factory with five pounds or less of refrigerant. Check the actual appliance evidence. A system with a small charge is not automatically a small appliance if the other parts of the definition are absent. Recovery requirements depend on the equipment and the condition of the appliance compressor. Under EPA's small-appliance service guidance, equipment manufactured before November 15, 1993 is associated with an eighty-percent recovery requirement. For equipment manufactured on or after that date, the requirement is ninety percent when the appliance compressor operates and eighty percent when it does not. The four-inches-of-mercury-vacuum alternative is also described in the applicable guidance. Distinguish a vacuum measurement from positive gauge pressure, and use a suitable calibrated instrument and the required instructions. Do not turn these percentages into pressure readings. Worked example: the nameplate charge is ten ounces and the recovery equipment is post-1993. If the compressor functions, ninety percent corresponds to nine ounces. If it does not function, eighty percent corresponds to eight ounces. This arithmetic explains the percentage; it does not replace the actual required field procedure or measurement method. A scale reading must be interpreted in the context of the equipment instructions and the actual refrigerant being recovered. Before practical recovery, identify the refrigerant, inspect the appliance and equipment, confirm compatibility, check the recovery container and its permitted use, and review the recovery machine's directions. Use the specified protective measures and manage electrical and ignition risks according to the actual equipment and refrigerant. Stop for an unidentified refrigerant, a damaged connection, incompatible recovery equipment, or an unsafe work area. Do not improvise a connection or a maximum container fill value. A qualified trainer must demonstrate the real equipment-specific connection, operation, verification, and safe disconnection. The learner then repeats those actions under the appropriate supervision. A stock clip of a technician holding gauges or a photograph of a refrigerator is contextual material; it does not establish that the learner has seen or performed the recovery procedure. Guided practice: select the applicable recovery target from the equipment date and compressor condition, explaining both pieces of evidence. Independent practice: classify a factory-sealed appliance, calculate a sample percentage, identify a stop condition, and describe which equipment instructions are still needed before work. Common mistakes include reversing the ninety/eighty decision, calling five pounds a minimum, treating the vacuum alternative as positive pressure, and claiming practical mastery from a quiz. Correct those mistakes using the nameplate, official requirements, recovery-equipment instructions, and trainer observation. Recap: classify the appliance, select the applicable requirement, use compatible certified equipment and its actual procedure, verify completion, and retain the practical checkoff separately from the online assessment.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: High-Pressure Appliances: Recovery, Leaks, Evacuation and Practice
prompts: Build a Type II evacuation-table worksheet from the current EPA service-practice table. Include appliance category, charge range, equipment date, required level, units, and pressure reference.
Compare leak detection, refrigerant recovery, and dehydration evacuation. Draw the distinct purpose of each stage.

Create two rule-identification scenarios distinguishing Section 608 ozone-depleting-refrigerant requirements from applicable AIM Act HFC requirements. Record source dates and avoid assuming every appliance has identical thresholds.
chapters.heading: Type II: table selection, leak rules, and pressure references
chapters.text: The Type II certificate scope includes high- and very-high-pressure appliances outside the small-appliance and MVAC exceptions. The service-practice evacuation table uses finer appliance categories; do not assume its 'high' and 'medium' rows are interchangeable. Under the current table, very-high-pressure appliances require 0 inches Hg vacuum; high-pressure appliances below 200 pounds require 0. High-pressure appliances at 200 pounds or more use 4 inches with pre-1993 equipment and 10 with post-1993 equipment. Medium-pressure appliances below 200 pounds use 4 and 10; those at 200 pounds or more use 4 and 15. Check the exact table and exception conditions before applying a row. Zero psig is approximately atmospheric pressure, not a deep vacuum. At standard atmosphere, psia = psig + 14.7. Never energize a hermetic compressor under vacuum. For the Section 608 ozone-depleting-refrigerant leak framework, the full-charge threshold is 50 pounds and the annual trigger rates are 30 percent industrial process, 20 percent commercial refrigeration, and 10 percent comfort cooling or other appliances. Applicable HFC requirements under the AIM Act have a different scope; identify the rule first rather than applying the ODS table to every system.
chapters.example: The worksheet states a medium-pressure appliance with a 250-pound full charge and post-1993 recovery equipment. The selected table value is 15 inches Hg vacuum. Changing the category to high pressure changes the selected value to 10. Changing only an unlabeled number is not adequate evidence: category, charge, date, units, and reference must travel together.
chapters.review: Compare recovery evacuation with dehydration and keep the legal leak-rate framework distinct from certification scope.

lessons.heading: Identify Type II scope from the appliance
lessons.text: Type II covers high-pressure and very-high-pressure stationary appliances except small appliances and motor vehicle air conditioners. Do not classify a system as Type II solely because it contains more than an invented number of pounds. Charge size can matter to a particular service requirement without defining the certification category. Read the equipment identification, refrigerant information and applicable certification definitions. Confirm whether the appliance meets all parts of the small-appliance definition before excluding it. A learner who has completed this lesson still needs the separate approved examination for certification and the qualifications required for the actual work.

lessons.heading: Select the applicable recovery requirement
lessons.text: Recovery requirements vary with appliance classification, charge and the recovery equipment's manufacturing date. Consult the current EPA table and the manufacturer's instructions for the actual appliance and task. Carefully distinguish inches of mercury vacuum, pounds per square inch gauge and absolute pressure. A number without its units and reference is incomplete. Do not copy the small-appliance eighty or ninety percent rule into every Type II scenario. Check whether an exception actually applies and document its conditions rather than using an exception as a general shortcut. Compatible certified recovery equipment must be operated according to its instructions.

lessons.heading: Keep three service activities distinct
lessons.text: Leak detection identifies where refrigerant is escaping. Recovery removes refrigerant into a suitable external container. Dehydration evacuation removes air and moisture after the circuit is appropriately prepared for that procedure. These activities have different purposes and cannot be treated as interchangeable. A vacuum pump is not a substitute for a refrigerant recovery machine. Recharging alone does not locate a leak, and an achieved recovery target does not prove a system is dry, leak-free or correctly charged. Identify the permitted test medium, pressure rating, ventilation and instrument requirements from the exact equipment and refrigerant documentation before supervised work.

lessons.heading: Check the current leak-repair rule before applying it
lessons.text: Different refrigerant regulations have different scopes. EPA's HFC leak-repair provisions began applying to affected appliances in January 2026; they include a fifteen-pound full-charge threshold and specified refrigerant conditions, with the residential and light-commercial air-conditioning and heat-pump subsector excluded. Those provisions must not be confused with the Section 608 ozone-depleting-refrigerant leak-repair framework. A technician must verify the refrigerant, appliance subsector, full charge, applicable rule and current effective requirements before choosing a compliance action. The absence of one rule's repair obligation does not grant permission for prohibited venting or unsafe work. Use the official rule and qualified compliance guidance for the actual job.

lessons.heading: Practice an evidence-based service decision
lessons.text: Consider a stationary high-pressure system with a suspected leak. Your task is to prepare a decision record, not connect gauges without authorization. List the appliance and refrigerant identification, full charge, certification scope, recovery equipment information and relevant manufacturer procedure. State which official table or rule you need, what units it uses and whether the available facts support a particular requirement. Then separate the proposed leak test, recovery, repair, evacuation and charging activities in the job plan. Mark missing evidence and unsafe conditions as stop points. Review the record with the instructor and retain practical performance assessment separately from the online knowledge result.

chapters.imageAlt: Technician Testing Industrial Air Conditioning with Multimeter

chapters.title: Low-Pressure Appliances: Recovery, Purging, Safety and Practice
prompts: Draw how a below-atmospheric-pressure chiller can admit air and moisture. Explain what excessive purging may suggest and what it cannot prove alone.
Explain the difference between 25 mm Hg absolute, inches Hg vacuum, and psig. Identify which reference belongs to the applicable low-pressure recovery requirement.

Research the reasons for controlling water-freezing risk during recovery and recharging. Prepare a trainer-question sheet covering vapor versus liquid introduction, equipment limits, and required supervision.
chapters.heading: Type III: air intrusion, freezing protection, and recovery
chapters.text: A low-pressure chiller may operate below atmospheric pressure. A leak can admit air and moisture instead of visibly releasing refrigerant. Noncondensables may increase condensing pressure and purge activity; these are clues to investigate, not automatic proof of one failed part. The applicable low-pressure recovery table value is 25 millimeters Hg absolute, approximately 25,000 microns, not 25 inches Hg vacuum or 25 psig. Recovering liquid first can reduce the amount remaining for vapor recovery, but vapor recovery still matters. Removing refrigerant can cool water and tubes enough to create freezing risk; water circulation or removal must follow the chiller's approved procedure. Charging may require vapor first to establish an appropriate condition before liquid is admitted, preventing freezing damage. Do not convert this principle into an equipment-independent connection sequence. For low-pressure leak testing, use the permitted controlled heating or pressurization method and manufacturer limits; never attach an arbitrary high-pressure source. Refrigerant monitoring, ventilation, and mechanical-room requirements protect occupants. Purge equipment removes unwanted noncondensables while minimizing refrigerant loss; it is not an unrestricted vent.
chapters.example: A display shows 25 without units. It cannot establish the recovery target. If the instrument is in mm Hg absolute, it expresses a very different condition from 25 psig. Before interpreting the reading, identify units, reference, calibration, instrument range, appliance category, and applicable service task.
chapters.review: Explain how freezing risk, air intrusion, and absolute-pressure measurement make low-pressure service distinct.

lessons.heading: Recognize low-pressure equipment and Type III
lessons.text: Type III certification covers low-pressure appliances. A low-pressure chiller is not classified as Type III because it exceeds a made-up charge minimum, and Type III does not mean high-pressure service. Identify the appliance and refrigerant from reliable documentation and review the certification definition applicable to it. Large vessels, water circuits and specialized controls may be present, but appearance alone is not the legal classification. Read the exact equipment service instructions and determine who is qualified to perform the work. This lesson prepares you to recognize decisions and hazards; it does not replace supervised chiller training or the separate approved EPA examination.

lessons.heading: Understand air intrusion and purging
lessons.text: Parts of a low-pressure system can operate below atmospheric pressure, allowing air and moisture to enter through leaks. Noncondensable gases can affect operation, while moisture can create further service problems. Purge equipment addresses unwanted noncondensables through the equipment-specific process; it is not permission to release refrigerant deliberately. Follow the manufacturer's purge-system instructions and applicable containment requirements. An unusual purge pattern can be evidence that further investigation is needed, but it does not identify every possible fault on its own. Record observations and compare them with equipment specifications instead of improvising a generic purge duration or venting procedure.

lessons.heading: Read recovery values with the correct pressure reference
lessons.text: EPA's stationary service table lists twenty-five millimeters of mercury absolute for low-pressure appliances under its applicable evacuation requirements. Absolute pressure is referenced to a vacuum, so this value must not be interpreted as twenty-five inches of mercury vacuum or twenty-five pounds per square inch gauge. A suitable instrument and the applicable instructions are essential. The small-appliance eighty and ninety percent alternatives are not a Type III recovery rule. Select the procedure for the actual service activity and verify any applicable exception from its conditions. Reaching a number in a study example does not prove that every required field step has been completed.

lessons.heading: Plan around equipment-specific hazards
lessons.text: Low-pressure chiller work may involve refrigerant exposure, oxygen displacement, electrical energy, rotating equipment and freezing damage to heat exchangers during certain service conditions. The actual refrigerant safety data, mechanical-room provisions and manufacturer instructions control the protective measures. Do not enter a potentially hazardous atmosphere or treat an ordinary face covering as protection from oxygen deficiency. Do not add heat, change water flow, pressurize a vessel or open a circuit from a generic classroom description. Those actions require the correct procedure, compatible equipment and qualified supervision. Stop when the refrigerant, instrument reference, vessel condition or safe work arrangements cannot be verified.

lessons.heading: Practice a low-pressure decision record
lessons.text: An instructor provides a chiller description and a worksheet displaying a recovery reading with no unit label. Explain why the reading cannot yet establish compliance. Request the instrument units, absolute or gauge reference, equipment classification and the applicable service procedure. Next, describe why a system operating below atmospheric pressure can draw air inward through a leak. Separate that explanation from an unsupported diagnosis of a particular component. Finish a pre-work checklist containing equipment documents, refrigerant identification, safety controls, selected recovery requirement and required supervisor. Keep your written response and corrections as learning evidence; actual operating and practical check-offs remain separate and must be observed.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: Core and Types I, II and III: Comparison and Final Practice
prompts: Create a four-column Core, Type I, Type II, and Type III study map. Assign environmental, legal, recovery, safety, and appliance-specific topics to their appropriate columns.
Write a correction log for five practice errors: the original reasoning, corrected reasoning, supporting source, and a new example.
Complete an exam-readiness checklist covering all four sections, pressure-temperature charts, measurement units, allowed exam materials, and the exam version scheduled by the testing provider.
chapters.heading: Build exam readiness by section rather than one average
chapters.text: Treat Core, Type I, Type II, and Type III as separate knowledge domains. A strong score in one area should not conceal a weak area in another. This workbook uses separate internal practice tests with an 80-percent training threshold. That threshold is an Elevate learning requirement; it is not a statement of the testing provider's certification rules. Work the questions without looking at notes, then use the explanations to repair specific misconceptions. For each missed item, write the concept, the reason your choice was wrong, a source or lesson reference, and a new example. Return to the diagram that represents the process instead of memorizing the position of a correct option. Confirm the exam version, allowed reference chart, identification requirements, location, and proctor arrangements with the testing provider. An internal practice pass does not record an external exam pass, and it does not waive hands-on assessment.
chapters.example: A student earns 96 percent Core, 88 percent Type I, 64 percent Type II, and 84 percent Type III. The overall average is above 80, but the Type II training requirement has not been met. The correct next step is focused Type II review and a new attempt, not averaging away the gap.
chapters.review: Use your weakest section and error log to choose the next study session.

lessons.heading: Separate Core knowledge from appliance categories
lessons.text: Core knowledge supports refrigerant handling across certification types: environmental effects, identification, containment, safety and service principles. Type I covers small appliances, Type II covers high- and very-high-pressure appliances except small appliances and motor vehicle air conditioners, and Type III covers low-pressure appliances. Universal covers all three categories. Passing this course's review does not award EPA certification; an approved examination and its applicable requirements are separate. Motor vehicle air-conditioning certification under Section 609 has its own scope. Write the appliance category and evidence first, then identify the relevant certification instead of choosing a category from a guessed charge threshold.

lessons.heading: Classify from all the necessary facts
lessons.text: A small appliance must be fully manufactured, charged and hermetically sealed in a factory with five pounds or less of refrigerant. A field-assembled stationary system with a four-pound charge does not meet that definition from weight alone. A low-pressure chiller is a Type III example because of its appliance category, not because a classroom problem assigns a large charge. For an unfamiliar appliance, obtain the nameplate, refrigerant information and applicable definition. If those facts are absent, identify the missing evidence. Choosing an answer without enough information is a study error and can become a safety or compliance error in the field.

lessons.heading: Compare recovery decisions without mixing rules
lessons.text: Small-appliance recovery decisions include eighty or ninety percent conditions based on recovery-equipment date and compressor operation, along with the applicable vacuum alternative. Other appliances use the relevant evacuation table and task requirements. Low-pressure table values use an absolute-pressure reference that must not be confused with inches of vacuum or positive gauge pressure. Recovery captures refrigerant, recycling processes it for reuse through applicable cleaning, and reclamation establishes the required purity through an EPA-certified reclaimer when required. None of those words means that an unknown mixture may be used in any appliance. Keep refrigerants identified and use compatible equipment and containers.

lessons.heading: Use mistakes to build a focused study plan
lessons.text: Review an incorrect response by naming the distinction you missed, not by memorizing the correct option's position. For example, if you chose Type III for a high-pressure system, revise the category comparison. If you chose ninety percent for every recovery task, return to the appliance-specific conditions. If you treated a gauge value as absolute pressure, review instrument units and references. If you selected a refrigerant only because it has lower warming impact, review compatibility and permitted use. Record the official source or equipment instruction that resolves the issue. Rework a different scenario to show that you understand the reason.

lessons.heading: Complete the comparison exercise and readiness review
lessons.text: Prepare four columns headed Core, Type I, Type II and Type III. Under each appliance type, enter its scope, the evidence needed to classify an example and the source used to select its recovery requirement. Under Core, list the identification, containment and safety concepts shared across the examples. Work the lesson's questions, explain every correction and ask the instructor to review unresolved topics before the separate approved exam. Keep knowledge results, supervised practical records and external certificates as different evidence items. Do not mark an external examination or hands-on skill complete because you watched a film, answered practice questions or finished an online progress bar.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: Charging, Gauges, Leak Detection and Recovery Practice
prompts: Use the virtual bench to create three hypothetical sets of saturation and line temperatures. Show superheat and subcooling calculations and units.
Draw a diagnostic sequence that checks airflow, measurement location, refrigerant identification, and manufacturer specifications before drawing a charge conclusion.
Compare an electronic leak detector, a recovery machine, and a vacuum pump. Explain why each has a different purpose and what evidence it can establish.
chapters.heading: Create a defensible diagnostic measurement sheet
chapters.text: Start a measurement sheet with appliance model, identified refrigerant, operating mode, outdoor and indoor conditions, and manufacturer reference. Record each reading at its actual measurement location with units and instrument details. Keep the raw readings separate from calculated values. A pressure reading does not establish refrigerant identity, charge correctness, airflow adequacy, or leak location on its own. Compare a hypothesis with multiple independent observations. Recovery captures refrigerant before the applicable circuit opening. Dehydration removes air and moisture from a properly prepared system; pressure measurement in that process requires the appropriate vacuum instrument and placement. A standing-vacuum observation is not interchangeable with every required pressure leak test. Use the exact approved method. This workbook's virtual instruments teach arithmetic and interpretation; they cannot reproduce every time-dependent effect, refrigerant property, or operating control of real equipment.
chapters.example: Suction saturation is supplied as 38 F and a matched vapor-line reading is 53 F, giving 15 F superheat. The student then discovers that the pressure was measured far from the temperature location. Keep the arithmetic in the record, label the interpretation unverified, and obtain the appropriate paired measurements under supervision.
chapters.review: Separate a raw reading, calculation, hypothesis, and verified diagnosis.

lessons.heading: Name the purpose before choosing a tool
lessons.text: Charging adds the specified refrigerant quantity or adjusts charge using the equipment's approved method. Leak detection seeks the location of an escape. Recovery removes refrigerant and stores it externally. Recycling cleans recovered refrigerant through the applicable process, while reclamation has a distinct purity and reclaimer framework. Dehydration evacuation addresses air and moisture after appropriate preparation. A manifold or gauge display does not perform all these functions by itself. Write the purpose of the proposed service step first, then select compatible equipment and the exact procedure. This distinction prevents a learner from treating a vacuum pump as a recovery machine or a pressure reading as proof of a complete diagnosis.

lessons.heading: Identify the system and the instrument
lessons.text: Before supervised refrigerant work, confirm appliance classification, refrigerant identity, charge information and manufacturer instructions. Verify the technician's required qualification and the compatibility, condition and ratings of hoses, gauges, temperature sensors, recovery equipment and containers. A fitting that connects does not prove suitability. Keep refrigerants identified and do not combine unknown contents. Read the instrument instructions, including the pressure reference and units. Gauge pressure and absolute pressure differ. For refrigerant blends, use the proper dew or bubble convention in the pressure-temperature information. Record what you measured and where, rather than copying an unlabeled number from a display.

lessons.heading: Interpret paired readings with a supported target
lessons.text: Pressure and temperature must be interpreted together with the refrigerant, operating mode, airflow, load and the manufacturer target method. In a hypothetical vapor-line example, a measured 55 degrees Fahrenheit and a corresponding saturation temperature of 42 produce 13 Fahrenheit degrees of superheat. That calculation does not prove a correct charge. A fixed-orifice appliance and a system using a different metering device may require different target methods. Check instrument placement and operating conditions before concluding that refrigerant is missing. Adding refrigerant to a system with an airflow problem can create a second fault and does not resolve the original cause.

lessons.heading: Plan leak testing and service controls
lessons.text: A leak investigation requires a compatible method, suitable instruments and the permitted test conditions. Never invent a universal test pressure or substitute oxygen or compressed air for the specified refrigerant-system test medium. Pressure ratings, refrigerant flammability and ventilation provisions matter. Recovery, repair, evacuation and charging must follow their respective instructions and containment requirements. Stop for an unidentified refrigerant, damaged hose, inappropriate container, unverified instrument setting or unsafe work area. Do not bypass an electrical protective device to keep equipment running during a test. A qualified supervisor must demonstrate the exact equipment-specific steps before the learner performs the practical work.

lessons.heading: Practice a complete service record
lessons.text: Prepare a worksheet for a system that is reported to cool poorly. Include the customer's concern, equipment identification, refrigerant, operating conditions, airflow observations, measurement locations and units. Explain which evidence is needed before selecting a charging action. Add separate boxes for leak detection, recovery, repair, evacuation and final verification; each box should identify its governing procedure and any missing information. Calculate the example superheat, then state why it cannot be used as a universal target. Review the worksheet with the instructor and correct unsupported conclusions. Retain observed practical check-offs separately: a correct paper calculation or viewed film does not establish that live refrigerant work was performed safely.

chapters.imageAlt: HVAC Technician Inspecting Air Conditioning System

chapters.title: Ductwork, Sizing, Brazing, Line Sets and System Startup
prompts: Sketch supply and return airflow paths and mark likely restrictions. Explain why an airflow problem can resemble a refrigerant problem.
Draw a line-set installation planning sheet: equipment identification, approved tubing, routing, support, joining, testing, and startup documentation. Mark every task requiring supervision.
Prepare a startup evidence checklist recording actual measurements and manufacturer targets separately. Explain why a generic workbook value cannot substitute for the equipment specifications.
chapters.heading: Connect installation planning with airside performance
chapters.text: Air moves because a fan establishes a pressure difference through a resistance network. Filters, coils, ducts, fittings, and grilles all contribute resistance. Supply and return paths must both be considered. Restricting return airflow can reduce delivered airflow even when the fan operates. Duct sizing and equipment selection require actual design information; a sketch alone cannot determine capacity. Refrigerant-line planning requires approved materials, length and elevation considerations, routing, supports, joining methods, and manufacturer requirements. Brazing adds heat and ignition risk and requires a qualified procedure, suitable area, and appropriate controls. Startup should verify installation conditions before evaluating performance. Record the specified target separately from the measured result and identify the source of the specification. Never label an installation acceptable because a single generic pressure resembles a workbook example.
chapters.example: A system starts and the supply grille feels cool, but a return duct is disconnected. 'Feels cool' does not verify an installation. Add the missing return-path inspection to the checklist and describe which operating measurements would be meaningful only after the installation condition is corrected.
chapters.review: Explain how a mechanical airside problem can change refrigerant-side observations.

lessons.heading: Begin sizing with the building load
lessons.text: Equipment capacity should follow a documented heating and cooling load calculation and an appropriate selection method. Floor area alone does not capture insulation, windows, orientation, air leakage, design conditions or internal loads. Oversizing is not a universal improvement: it can affect cycling, comfort, humidity control and cost. Obtain the design information and verify assumptions before selecting an appliance. The learner should be able to explain why two buildings with the same floor area can need different capacities. A classroom rule of thumb is not a substitute for the applicable load calculation, equipment selection process or required professional design review.

lessons.heading: Connect duct design to delivered airflow
lessons.text: A duct system must move the required air through the actual supply and return paths while accounting for the equipment's available pressure and component resistance. Duct length, fittings, filters, coils, grilles, leakage and restrictions influence performance. Replacing an appliance without checking the distribution system can leave the original comfort problem unresolved. Compare the planned layout and measured performance with the approved design and equipment specifications. Do not assign one duct diameter or one airflow value to every installation. Record the design basis, equipment settings and verification results so that the completed system can be evaluated using evidence.

lessons.heading: Prepare line sets and hot work correctly
lessons.text: Refrigerant piping materials, sizes, lengths, insulation and connection methods must follow the exact appliance instructions and applicable requirements. Keep tubing appropriately protected from contamination during preparation. Brazing introduces fire, burn and fume hazards and requires trained personnel, ventilation, suitable protective equipment and the site's hot-work controls. Remove or protect combustibles and establish any required fire watch and emergency arrangements. Never heat a charged or unprepared refrigerant circuit based on a classroom demonstration. Follow the applicable recovery and isolation procedures before authorized work. Refrigerant decomposition and, for some refrigerants, ignition hazards make the actual equipment and safety documentation essential.

lessons.heading: Distinguish purging, testing and evacuation
lessons.text: A specified nitrogen flow during brazing, a pressure test and dehydration evacuation are different operations with different equipment settings and purposes. Do not transfer a pressure or flow value from one operation to another. Use the permitted gas, regulator, pressure protection and procedure for the exact task; oxygen or compressed air must not be improvised as refrigerant-system test gas. Nitrogen can displace oxygen, so ventilation and atmosphere hazards still matter. Stop when the test medium, ratings, recovery condition, hot-work safeguards or supervision cannot be confirmed. An online explanation cannot replace a qualified demonstration and observed practical performance.

lessons.heading: Document startup rather than declaring success from sound
lessons.text: Prepare a startup checklist using the actual equipment instructions. It may include verified installation details, electrical checks by qualified personnel, controls, airflow, drain operation, refrigerant checks, safety devices and recorded operating conditions. Confirm which checks apply to the installed configuration and obtain the required review before operation. A fan or compressor running is not proof that the installation is complete. In a practice scenario, identify one missing design assumption, one duct restriction, one hot-work stop condition and one startup measurement that needs a stated target.
